questions.q: What is one effective way to make a Tableau extract smaller and faster?
options: Hide unused fields and filter the extract to only the rows actually needed before extracting
Add every available field to the extract, whether or not it's used
Switch the extract to a live connection instead
Disable incremental refresh so the extract always processes everything
questions.explain: Hiding unused fields and filtering rows both shrink an extract's size directly, which speeds up both its refresh and how quickly Tableau can query it.

questions.q: What does a context filter actually do, and what's the caution around using it?
options: It's computed once so other filters run against its reduced result, but it has its own recompute cost, so it should be reserved for filters genuinely shared across most sheets
It permanently deletes rows that don't match the filter from the data source
It has no performance cost and should be applied to every filter in a workbook
It only works on Tableau Public, not Tableau Server or Cloud
questions.explain: A context filter reduces the working data set once so other filters operate on less data, but computing that context itself has a cost — which is why it should be used deliberately, not on every filter.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which type of calculation is typically the most expensive at high row counts?
options: A FIXED LOD expression, because it's recomputed against the underlying level of detail
A simple row-level calculation like [Sales] minus [Cost]
A basic SUM aggregation
A calculated field with no functions at all
questions.explain: FIXED LOD expressions can be expensive at scale because they recompute against the underlying detail level, unlike simple row-level or standard aggregate calculations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend using actions instead of universal quick filters on a dashboard where possible?
options: An action only re-queries the specific sheets it targets, instead of every sheet on the dashboard reacting to every filter change
Actions eliminate the need for any data source entirely
Quick filters are always visually worse than actions
Actions only work with extracts, never live connections
questions.explain: Because an action targets specific sheets rather than triggering every sheet on the dashboard to re-query, it reduces the total query load an interaction causes.

questions.q: What is the recommended workflow this lesson ties together with Lesson 90?
options: Record performance, apply a targeted fix from the checklist, then record again to confirm the fix actually helped
Apply every optimization technique at once without measuring anything
Only optimize calculations, since they are always the slowest part of a workbook
Skip Performance Recording entirely once you've read the checklist
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes a loop: measure, fix the top offender, then re-measure to confirm the fix worked — optimizing without re-measuring is just as much guessing as never measuring at all.
